Approximate VIX is the 30-day variance-swap rate built from five points on the 30-day constant-maturity smile (5- and 25-delta calls, at-the-money, 25- and 5-delta puts), with vol linear in log-strike between them, flat beyond the 5-delta call, and on the put side continuing the 25-to-5-delta slope up to twice the 5-delta vol. For SPX it runs about 0.3 points under VIX on average (mean absolute gap 0.6). The surface is snapped shortly before the close, so on fast days it can differ from VIX's close. The SPX smile has no wing points for most of 2013-2019; those days use SPY (about 0.3 points higher), and no split is made across a switch. Each day's change is split four ways, each factor's share averaged over every order of applying them, so they add up exactly: spot, the at-the-money change from rolling along yesterday's smile to today's price (sticky strike); parallel, the rest of the at-the-money change; skew, the change in the 25-delta put and call vols relative to at-the-money; convexity, the change in the 5-delta wings relative to the 25-delta points. Skew is measured in delta space, so it is not the same as a fixed-strike decomposition. The 5-delta put is noisy from day to day, which shows up as alternating convexity bars; sums over a few days are steadier. Skew ratio: 25-delta put vol / 25-delta call vol. Put convexity: 5-delta put vol / 25-delta put vol.
